### Hybrid Vision Transformer Architectures for Visuo-Motor Control

Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong performance in computer vision through large-scale pretraining, but their weak inductive biases—specifically the lack of spatial locality and translation equivariance—hinder their effectiveness in visuo-motor control tasks where these biases are critical. To address this, researchers have developed hybrid architectures that incorporate control-centric biases into ViTs. One approach involves designing specialized transformer architectures for control. For example, CtrlFormer <cite>Mu et al., 2022</cite> learns transferable state representations by jointly attending to visual and policy tokens across tasks, improving sample efficiency but not directly addressing ViT's inherent bias limitations. Thomas et al. (2023) introduce MVP (Masked Visual Pre-training for Motor Control), a method that uses Vision Transformers (ViTs) and masked autoencoders (MAE) to learn visual representations for motor control from large datasets of human-object interaction images. These methods enhance multi-task learning but do not explicitly inject the locality and equivariance needed for robust control.

Another strategy focuses on adapting pretrained ViTs without compromising their original capabilities. Sharma et al. <cite>Sharma et al., 2023</cite> propose lossless adaptation with parameter-efficient adapters to prevent representational drift during fine-tuning, preserving model versatility but not augmenting inductive biases. Qian et al. (2024) introduce SATA, a method that enhances Vision Transformer (ViT) robustness and efficiency in image classification by analyzing and grouping tokens based on their spatial autocorrelation scores. Liang et al. (2024) introduce PLEX, a transformer-based architecture for robotic manipulation that leverages diverse data sources, including video-only data and visuomotor trajectories, to achieve general robotic manipulation. These adaptations improve utility but fall short in directly embedding control-centric biases into ViT architectures.

In contrast, our Convolution Injector (CoIn) directly injects convolutions into pretrained ViTs, providing built-in spatial locality and translation equivariance. This modular add-on compensates for ViT shortcomings more fundamentally than prior methods, leading to consistent performance gains across diverse control tasks without extensive retraining or external processing.

### Representation Learning for Visuo-Motor Policy Generalization

Generalizable visuo-motor policies require robust visual representations that transfer across varying environments and tasks. Many approaches learn invariances through specialized architectures or training techniques. The choice of pre-training datasets significantly impacts the performance of visual representations in robotics, with some studies indicating that traditional vision datasets can even outperform specialized robot learning datasets for this purpose <cite>Yang et al., 2023</cite>. The provided source for Florence et al. (2019) describes OpenVLA, a 7B-parameter open-source Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that leverages pretrained vision-language models and fine-tunes them on large robot demonstration datasets for generalist robot manipulation. These techniques enhance robustness but often require significant architectural changes or additional training objectives.

Pretrained visual representations (PVRs) are widely used to boost generalization, with studies highlighting their transfer potential. Silwal et al. <cite>Silwal et al., 2023</cite> investigate the adaptation of pre-trained visual representations (PVRs) for downstream control tasks in robotic manipulation, proposing learning human-inspired perceptual skills to guide representation learning. Huo et al. (2023) focus on improving the generalization of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods for adapting pre-trained transformers to downstream tasks, enhancing generalization and retaining knowledge from large-scale pre-training by regularizing gradients and aligning fine-tuned models with their pre-trained counterparts. Similarly, CtrlFormer <cite>Mu et al., 2022</cite> aims for sample-efficient multi-task and cross-robot transfer by learning transferable representations through multi-task attention or data fusion. PLEX <cite>Thomas et al., 2023</cite> also learns transferable representations, but both approaches may still face challenges in fully addressing bias gaps in standard ViTs.

Further efforts tackle generalization challenges like sim-to-real transfer and sample efficiency. Zhang et al. <cite>Zhang et al., 2016</cite> use modular networks with perception-control bottlenecks for sim-to-real transfer, but their methods are not tailored to ViTs. Zhao et al. <cite>Zhao et al., 2024</cite> introduce control-aware augmentation and distillation to improve policy generalization, yet they focus on training strategies rather than model architecture. Chen et al. (BYOVLA) focus on improving the visual generalization of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by minimally altering visual inputs at runtime to reduce sensitivity to distractors, thereby addressing robustness to visual distractors. Tao et al. <cite>Tao et al., 2022</cite> introduce locality into Vision Transformers (ViTs) to enhance their data efficiency, particularly on smaller datasets, aiming to make them more competitive with CNNs under limited data conditions.

Our CoIn module directly enhances pretrained ViTs with control-centric biases, improving representation quality for policy generalization without the overhead of complex adaptations or auxiliary tasks. By integrating convolutions, CoIn offers a more efficient path to robust visuo-motor policies compared to methods that rely solely on data augmentation or external modules.

While my work addresses the lack of control-centric inductive biases in pretrained ViTs for visuo-motor control, CtrlFormer tackles the broader challenge of transfer learning across different control tasks and robotic embodiments. Specifically, CtrlFormer's approach to aligning observation and action spaces across robots, and its use of separate policy heads for individual robot dynamics, contrasts with my method of injecting convolutional biases into a single ViT for improved adaptation. Both works leverage Transformers for visual control, but CtrlFormer emphasizes multi-robot generalization and sample efficiency through its unique architecture and contrastive learning paradigm, whereas my work focuses on enhancing the inductive biases of existing pretrained ViTs.
